what_its_for: Atazanavir is an antiviral medicine used to treat HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) infection in adults and children. It belongs to a group of medicines called protease inhibitors. It works by blocking an enzyme that HIV needs to make copies of itself, which helps lower the amount of HIV in your body and keeps your immune system stronger. Atazanavir does not cure HIV, but it helps control the infection.
how_to_take: Take atazanavir by mouth exactly as your doctor tells you. Always take it WITH food — this helps your body absorb the medicine better. Swallow the capsules whole. Do not open, crush, or chew the capsules unless your doctor or pharmacist tells you to. If you are taking the powder form, mix it with food or liquid as directed. Atazanavir is almost always taken along with another medicine called ritonavir (Norvir) or cobicistat to help it work properly — do not stop taking either medicine without talking to your doctor first.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 300 mg (one capsule) once a day, taken with ritonavir 100 mg. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on your other medicines, kidney or liver function, or other health conditions. For children, the dose is based on body weight and will be determined by your doctor. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is within 6 hours of when you normally take it. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. Taking doses on schedule is very important with HIV medicines — missing doses can allow the virus to multiply and become harder to treat.
storage: Store atazanavir capsules at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep the bottle tightly closed. Store away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids, stomach acid reducers (like omeprazole, lansoprazole, or ranitidine), or heartburn medicines too close to your atazanavir dose, as these can prevent it from being absorbed properly — ask your doctor or pharmacist for specific timing guidance. Do not take St. John's Wort, as it can make atazanavir stop working. Avoid drinking large amounts of alcohol. Do not take sildenafil (Viagra) for pulmonary arterial hypertension while on atazanavir without your doctor's approval, as it can cause dangerous side effects. Always tell ALL your doctors and pharmacists that you take atazanavir before starting any new medicine, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements, because many medications can interact with it.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience: yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice), severe stomach or back pain, nausea and vomiting that won't stop, dark urine or pale stools, signs of kidney stones such as sharp pain in your back or side, blood in urine, or pain when urinating, unusual muscle pain or weakness, changes in your heartbeat (fast, slow, or irregular), signs of a serious skin reaction such as a rash with blisters, peeling skin, or sores in your mouth, signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst or urination, or any signs of a severe allergic reaction such as swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also contact your doctor if you notice fat redistribution (changes in body fat), increased cholesterol levels, or feel that the medicine is not working.
when_it_works: Atazanavir starts working in your body shortly after you begin taking it, but you may not feel any different right away. After a few weeks of treatment, blood tests should show that the amount of HIV in your blood (called viral load) is decreasing and your CD4 cell count (immune cells) is improving. It may take several months of consistent daily use to reach the best results. It is very important to keep taking your medicine every day, even if you feel well, because stopping can allow the virus to multiply again.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Atazanavir can be used during pregnancy but your doctor may adjust the dose. If you are pregnant and HIV-positive, staying on treatment is important to protect both you and your baby. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed if you have HIV, as the virus can be passed to the baby through breast milk. Children: Atazanavir can be used in children at least 3 months old and weighing at least 5 kg (about 11 lbs). Doses are based on weight. Kidney/Liver Problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, including hepatitis B or C. Atazanavir may require dose adjustments or may not be recommended in certain liver conditions. Older Adults: Older patients should use this medicine with caution and may be more sensitive to side effects — your doctor will monitor you closely.
